<meta>This page continues the discussion on the regulations of meat consumption and animal slaughter from the Laws of Manu, specifically focusing on permitted substitutes for meat and the spiritual consequences of unnecessary violence.</meta>

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** When there is an absolutely intense and overwhelming craving for eating meat, even then that desire should be satisfied by other means, for killing an animal is never proper. One should use a <term>ghṛta-paśu</term> <gloss>ghee-animal</gloss>, which is a preparation of clarified butter made to resemble the form of animal meat. Likewise, one may use a <term>piṣṭa-paśu</term> <gloss>flour-animal</gloss>. The term <term>saṅge</term> <gloss>in attachment</gloss> refers to having an extreme desire. Some interpret this attachment as being overcome by spirits, but this is not the commonly accepted meaning in the world, so the first explanation is better.

( 3 ) **Kullūka:** If there is an addiction or a strong passion for eating meat, one should make an image of an animal out of ghee or flour and eat that. One should never desire to kill animals at any time without a purpose related to the deities.

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda:** A <term>ghṛta-paśu</term> is a replica of an animal made of clarified butter. This substitute is used <term>saṅge</term> <gloss>in attachment</gloss>, meaning when there is a persistent urge for meat or a strong desire for consumption. This applies to mandatory domestic rituals <note>Smārta acts</note>, but not to Vedic sacrifices, because in Vedic rites, the use of a ghee-animal would interfere with the specific rules regarding the eleven portions of the victim. Therefore, it is said that "killing in a sacrifice is not considered killing."

( 5 ) **Nandana:** He explains that one should not commit violence except as prescribed. In the context of a <term>saṅga</term> <gloss>gathering</gloss>, such as a festival or a meeting of kinsmen, one should offer a ghee-animal. In place of a real animal, one should provide a large quantity of ghee and flour-cakes.

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra:** One should use a ghee-animal when there is a strong attachment. One should similarly use a flour-animal. One should never wish to kill an animal in vain.

### For as many hairs as there are on the animal, so many times the one who kills an animal in vain shall suffer death in birth after birth in the afterlife. 38

( 1 ) **Medhātithi:** The killer undergoes the cycle of death for that many births. A <term>vṛthā-paśughna</term> <gloss>one who kills an animal in vain</gloss> is one who performs animal slaughter that is not commanded by the Vedas or the traditional laws. In this context, this refers to hunters and others who kill for worldly purposes. The word <term>paśughna</term> <gloss>animal-killer</gloss> is a Vedic grammatical form.

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** "So many times" means that specific number of occurrences. A "vain killer" is one not authorized by the Vedas or traditional law.

( 3 ) **Kullūka:** He who kills animals for his own sake without intending them for a deity is called a "vain killer." After death, he suffers death in as many future births as there are hairs on the animal's body. Therefore, one should not kill an animal in vain. The word <term>ha</term> in the verse is used to indicate a well-known tradition or scriptural truth.

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda:** He describes the punishment for the opposing view. Here, the word <term>ha</term> highlights a well-known fact.

( 5 ) **Nandana:** "So many times" means that many instances. The word <term>ha</term> is used here to express compassion.

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra:** A man who kills an animal in vain performs an unrighteous act of killing in this world. For as many hairs as there are—estimated at eighty million hairs—he will attain the state of an animal and experience death for that many times in birth after birth in the afterlife.

### Animals were created for the sake of sacrifice by the Self-Existent One himself; for the prosperity of this entire world; therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not considered killing. 39

( 1 ) **Medhātithi:** This explains why the previously mentioned fault does not apply here. Animals were created by the <term>svayambhū</term> <gloss>Self-Existent One, Prajāpati</gloss> specifically for the prosperity that comes from the violence commanded by the Vedas and traditional laws as part of a sacrifice. The phrase "by himself" is a form of praise <note>arthavāda</note>. Sacrifice, such as the <term>Jyotiṣṭoma</term>, is for the <term>bhūti</term> <gloss>prosperity, power, or nourishment</gloss> of this whole universe. Therefore, the killing that happens there should be understood as "non-killing." This is said to show the absence of the sin that usually arises from violence.

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** He removes the doubt of how there is no such fault in killing for sacrifice. It is for the prosperity or "birth" of the world. Through the offerings, the sun is nourished, which leads to rain, then to seeds, and through the sequence of procreation, to the birth of living beings. By this, it is said that there is no fault because by the sacrifice of one animal, many living beings are sustained.

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual penalties for killing animals for personal pleasure and introduces the concept of using ghee or flour substitutes. It concludes by justifying ritual sacrifice as a divine institution intended for the nourishment and prosperity of the entire world.</summary>
